25 more ideas
  • Pascal's triangle mod 7 as a triangle (x > y black): row 7 vanishes to 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 1. Sibling of lattice-paths.
  • Pascal's triangle mod 3: a Sierpinski-like fractal in black, white and red.
  • Pisano periods: F(8y + x) mod 7 has period 16, so the odd rows are the negation of the even rows. F mod 3 has period 8, so every row is identical (a trap).
  • Gaussian primes: x^2 + y^2 prime, colored by p % 8. Only 1, 5 and red (2) appear (Fermat's two-square theorem), and prime cells sit on one checkerboard color. Sparse picture.
  • Hanoi ruler function: v2((x+1)*(y+1)) = v2(x+1) + v2(y+1), a tartan plaid.
  • Days per month over 64 months from Jan 2023 via the knuckle formula 30 + (m + m/8) % 2, with Feb 2024 leap. Mostly purple and blue noise.
  • Leap-year trap (1900 is not a leap year): too sparse on a 64-year window.
  • Greedy change with coins {25,10,5,1}: values fit in 0..7, but the picture is noisy.
  • Josephus table: j = (j + y + 1) % n for n = 2..x+1, one pass per row. Noisy picture.
  • Big-Omega (prime factors with multiplicity) of 8y + x + 1: values 0..6, a factoring grind.
  • Abundant, perfect and deficient via sigma(n): 6 and 28 perfect, all abundant numbers even. Too much grind.
  • Happy numbers (decimal) up to 64: long chains, sparse picture. The base-8 version has messy cycles.
  • McCarthy 91 scaled down: a scary double recursion that collapses to a constant. Too flat a picture.
  • Stern's diatomic sequence, Recaman's sequence, Hofstadter Q mod 8: hard and noisy.
  • Kolakoski sequence (self-describing runs of 1s and 2s): a white and red picture, maybe fits in 12 lines.
  • Zeckendorf: the number of Fibonacci terms in the greedy decomposition (0..4).
  • Digit sum of 8y + x in base 3: its parity equals n's parity. Noisy.
  • Unsigned range-check trap `(unsigned)(x - 2) < 4`: legal as-is, but a C-rules idea rather than numbers.
  • CRT search loop (n % 8 == x && n % 7 == y % 7) that collapses to diagonal stripes.
  • Discrete log mod 7 (powers of 3) turning the times table into an addition table.
  • Triangular numbers mod 8 are a permutation (0 1 3 6 2 7 5 4); T(x) + T(y) mod 8 gives a symmetric Latin square.
  • Snake counter: the boustrophedon index % 7 draws chevrons.
  • Tens digit of (x+1)*(y+1): easy hyperbola bands, too close to peasant.
  • Straight FizzBuzz (correct order), if the trap version runs first and players ask for the real one.
  • Perfect-shuffle variants: in-shuffle, or a 10-card deck (still periodic).

mechanics round 1

Rich. This pass produced 26 levels that pass the real pipeline, 16 of them traps. None repeats ideas the sibling agents already cover: Euclid, negative %, truncation toward zero, unsigned range checks, sizeof, designated initializers, octal, transposed tables, Life, bubble sort, Pascal mod 3, Sierpinski carpet, buggy prime, mirror recursion.

Two veins look close to inexhaustible:

  • Classic algorithms traced into a picture: binary search, hash probing, Josephus, Tetris line clear, rain water, turtle graphics, painter's algorithm, Langton's ant. Each gives a new image, and developers recognize them.
  • Classic bugs as fair traps: reverse twice, erase while iterating, swapped clamp, dead else-if, shadowed variable, Duff's count 0, default placement, case inside an if, a McCarthy-style collapse.

I estimate 40 to 60 more good levels from these two.

Limits:

  • gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror rejects most syntax-level traps (stray semicolons, dangling else, a < b < c, bitwise precedence, comma with no effect). Traps have to come from semantics: evaluation order, scope, fallthrough, loop and array bugs, integer rules.
  • Array levels drift toward bar charts; I already have five (duff-zero, castle-default, reverse-twice, rain-water, erase-while-iterating), so vary the display.
  • Traps lose their punch if they come too often; roughly one a week seems right.

Seen from mechanics, the current dailies barely use C beyond expressions. Only #7 and #9 loop, #10 and #11 index arrays, and nothing uses switch, recursion, do-while or short-circuit side effects. Both existing traps (#11 and #12) collapse to trivial pictures (x and y). A trap is more rewarding when the collapsed answer is still worth painting, as in reverse-twice, swapped-clamp, mccarthy or dead-else-if.

Candidate files are in /tmp/claude-1000/-home-lucien-dev-draw-my-code/6539cb5f-e2be-4d0a-a035-bf4a959a1c91/scratchpad/daily-design/mechanics/. Probes, including the rejected-trap tests, are in its probe/ subfolder.

  • Postfix binds tighter than %: (x + y) % 3[c] is (x + y) % c[3], not c[(x + y) % 3]. It compiles (tested); it needs a base picture that isn't diagonal stripes.
  • Tiny bytecode VM (enum opcodes, switch in a loop). It compiles and works, but add/halve/flip ops only give diagonal stripes that are tedious to paint; an op set with MAX or MIRROR might draw shapes.
  • goto jumping into a for body skips its init and first test: it compiles, but only one column changes. Also: goto state machines, and a goto retry loop over an LCG (gives a Latin square, too tedious).
  • AT&T 1990 bug: break inside a switch inside a loop only leaves the switch. It compiles; my picture was a dull column ramp.
  • Broken swap without a temp (x = y; y = x) collapses to f(y, y): rows, the same answer shape as #12.

pictures round 1

Pictures and games are a rich vein, probably the richest. I built 28 passing levels without exhausting it, and each strong mechanic opens a series: 2048 moves, Lights Out presses, Tetris clears, font-table numbers, identicon sprites, soroban numbers, Wordle rounds, Minesweeper formulas, game replays (Connect Four, snake paths). With variants, 60 or more good pictures and games seem reachable. The binding limits are the 12-by-36 frame (Mastermind, Life, Langton's ant and Hanoi don't fit) and the painting chore of scattered grids: Minesweeper, Wordle and traffic run to 24-34 strokes. The warning is the one the owner raised himself: sprites naturally reach for bit masks. 12 of my 28 decode bits (hex, octal, 64-bit, shifts, XOR), so cap them at about one a week and vary the decoding each time (decimal, octal, whole-grid-in-one-number, mirrored half rows, bit-parallel rules). The other 16 use arithmetic, loops and game rules only: soroban, dice, Connect Four, Wordle, rainbow, Minesweeper, 2048, sandpile, battery, plot, terrain, brick wall, mushroom, flag, melody, Tetris-by-rules. My strongest picks are 2048, lights-out, tetris-clear, battery, soroban, wordle, rainbow and connect-four, then tic-tac-toe, little-endian-smiley, snake, minesweeper and dice as solid mid-week levels. Brick-wall, union-flag, terrain and ode suit Mondays. Near-duplicate risk against the other agents: the cursor is a third hex-mask sprite, the heart repeats a subject, and Minesweeper exists there with coordinate arrays. I compared each grid with the 138 existing ones and with each other, including mirrors, rotations, recolorings and one-row or one-column shifts. The closest is at least 12 cells away (greedy color matching).

Difficulty runs from 2 to 4; none reached 5.

  • Strongest: look-and-say, busy-beaver, tromino-tiling, lz77-window, frogger, heap-icicle, fenwick-blocks, quadtree-diagonal, lcs-table, lru-cache, euclid-squares, two-pointers, nim-move.
  • Trap: xor-swap-selection, a new mechanism (the XOR swap zeroes a value swapped with itself). The naive reading is 18 cells off.
  • Easy Monday levels: water-jugs, first-fit, interval-scheduling, ring-buffer, merge-sort-passes, spiral-order.
  • Weaker, graded honestly in the notes: hash-chains (little picture), sliding-window-max, interval-scheduling (very regular). max-square-ball is tap-heavy (about 33 strokes).

Dropped during design:

  • Wordle and Mastermind: scoring repeated letters or colors correctly did not fit 12 lines of 36 columns.
  • Othello flips, Bomberman chains and bitboard flood fill: too long.
  • A trap where each colored cell repaints its row and column as the scan goes: the true grid was only plain blocks.
  • Falling sand: needed 13 lines.
  • Hilbert curve (coarse rectangles only), Dutch flag (dull) and the dragon curve (unrecognizable at 8x8).

mechanics round 2

I built 25 candidates for the mechanics key. The earlier drafts 01-23 in the same folder were left untouched; I reworked six of them into new files (night-sky, lit-floors, fallen-heart, padlock, battleship, inkblot) and kept four as-is (mondrian, rps-bracket, house, resistor). Each trap has a NN-slug.naive.c sibling built with plain gcc, and the cells-off counts in the traps come from comparing against it.

Brief coverage:

  • break inside a switch inside a loop: pawn.
  • continue in do-while: house.
  • goto used cleanly: padlock (a URL that is a label plus a comment), battleship, dead-code.
  • comma operator in a for: inkblot; resistor uses it in a while body.
  • unsigned wraparound: saucer, where squares survive the wrap.
  • % with negative numbers, new picture: kite.
  • shadowing: fallen-heart. It is the same C rule as ready/shadow-flag.c.
  • nested ternaries: mondrian.
  • a[i][j] index composition: kaleidoscope, invader, cube-turn, and stride-owl (a wrong row stride of 7 skews the stored image).
  • array read backwards: inkblot.
  • recursion with two calls: rps-bracket.
  • a loop that never runs: dead-code, where goto jumps into a while (0) body.

Mechanisms outside the brief list:

  • union: night-sky.
  • pointer aliasing: lit-floors.
  • 1-bit bit-field: linked-squares.
  • flag chain t & V & H: gingham.
  • =+ read as +=: bell.
  • missing return on a recursive call: sunset.
  • break leaving only the inner loop: crosshair.
  • digraphs: digraph-bolt.
  • y[w] subscript: wine-glass.
  • No existing level uses union, pointers, goto, break, 2D arrays, bit-fields, digraphs or =+.

Not covered:

  • sizeof, designated initializers, ternary versus + and short-circuit: the ungraded levels already use them, so I did not redo them.
  • enum gaps: daily 15 already has SEA = 7.
  • compound assignment order: a brute-force search found no fair trap with a picture worth painting.
  • true integer promotion: gcc rejects signed/unsigned mixes under -Wsign-compare, and short promotion depends on type width.
  • gcc under the level flags also rejects brace elision, dangling else, a stray ; after a for, and chained comparisons.

Quality:

  • Strongest: night-sky, padlock, lit-floors, pawn, inkblot, kaleidoscope, stride-owl.
  • Weaker: linked-squares, crosshair and gingham have abstract pictures or traps only just over 15 cells; digraph-bolt and wine-glass are syntax curiosities, not traps.
  • Alternates: invader repeats kaleidoscope's trap. Pawn, bell and wine-glass are similar centered silhouettes.

Collisions: nothing is above 55/64 against the existing grids (checked with rotations, mirrors, one-cell shifts and color swaps). Against the other round-2 folders, the closest are bell versus specials/08-fir-tree at 56/64 and pawn versus specials/04-april-fish at 55/64. I dropped an unsigned hourglass (the same picture as art-numbers/12-hourglass and specials/01-hourglass) and a stride ghost (identical to daily 27).

geometry round 2

I built 26 geometry candidates for round two. The repo was not touched.

For each grid I measured painting effort (colored cells, strokes = runs, isolated taps) and its similarity to all 138 existing grids, counting rotations, mirrors, recolorings and one-cell shifts. The helper scripts are in tools/ in that folder: ana.py computes these numbers, render.py draws sheet.png, the contact sheet.

Ranking. Candidates are listed from strongest to weakest.

  • Strongest: raycaster (the perspective idea), weave, trefoil, taxi-race, pinwheel-proof, bathroom-floor, saltire, euclid-squares.
  • Solid: cameras, hello-triangle, carroll, snail, pick, hex-rings, fox-and-hen, shadow-on-the-wall, leaf, rose, moves, detour, unit-balls.
  • Spares: plus-tiling, three-shears, honeycomb, triangle-sides, cake-cut.

Coverage of the requested ideas:

  • Apollonius: fox-and-hen.
  • 3-4-5: saltire uses |4v - 3u| < 7 (m + n - gcd).
  • Taxicab ellipse: detour.
  • Intercept theorem: shadow-on-the-wall and cameras.
  • Perspective: raycaster.
  • Point and rotational symmetry: pinwheel-proof and trefoil.
  • Hexagons on the square grid: hex-rings and honeycomb.
  • Cross-product angles: pick, cameras, trefoil.
  • Integer spiral: snail.
  • Pick's theorem: pick.
  • Triangle centers: hello-triangle (the medians meet at the centroid).

Ideas that didn't work at 8x8:

  • Perspective checkerboard floor: aliases into noise.
  • Knight in two moves: always a checkerboard, so about 40 taps.
  • Nightrider: sparse taps.
  • Parabola by focus and directrix: always a flat dome or a plain U.
  • Yin-yang: too coarse.
  • Bresenham, including the "a line drawn both ways differs" version: tap-heavy texture.
  • Orthocenter and incenter: triangles with nice lattice altitudes are tiny.
  • Also rejected:
    • Circle inversion, Cassini ovals, pentagram with even-odd fill: noise or crude shapes.
    • Tromino tiling: can't fit 12 lines.
    • Three-well Voronoi: the same skeleton as daily 34.
    • Three lines making seven regions: lopsided.
    • An arrow for three-shears: duplicates daily 9, so it uses a Tetris L.

Scheduling notes:

  • Circles: fox-and-hen, trefoil and unit-balls count toward "one circle every two weeks".
  • Sibling skeletons need to be kept weeks apart, or trimmed to one:
    • Linear form mod n picks a tile: plus-tiling, bathroom-floor, honeycomb.
    • Taxicab: taxi-race, detour, moves.
    • Edge functions: pick, hello-triangle.
    • pinwheel-proof and daily 37 / pool droste-twist (recursion folding the coordinates).
    • three-shears and daily 45 (both rotate a picture).
  • Similarity: the highest non-spare matches are shadow-on-the-wall at 0.86 (its wedge against two ungraded staircases) and unit-balls, three-shears and taxi-race at 0.80–0.82. Everything else is 0.79 or lower.
  • Traps: none turns on a C token; geometry traps kept being blocked by -Wall (chained comparisons, & precedence, dangling else). Three-shears has a lure: it looks like the add/subtract swap idiom, and reading it as a swap puts the L 16 cells off.
  • Specials: rose could be St Patrick's Day (#164, Wed Mar 17 2027) if painted all green with a stem. Trefoil and shadow-on-the-wall could be spooky alternatives.

art-numbers round 2

The grids here were copied from that output by a script, not retyped. The repo is untouched.

No candidate is closer than 57/64 to any of the 138 existing grids, even allowing rotations, mirrors, one-row or one-column shifts and any recoloring. The 57/64 match (calculator vs ternary-precedence) and the 51-53/64 ones are artifacts of mostly one-color grids, not real repeats. The worst pair among my own candidates is 48/64.

Strongest (self-grade A/A-):

  • Flags: south-africa (six colors from one distance), seychelles (rays as summed comparisons), greenland (!= as XOR, counterchange), jamaica (comparing two comparisons).
  • Pictures: calculator-hi (7-segment "14" read upside down), binary-tree-maze, pinwheel (recursion as a quarter turn).
  • Number art: octal-pascal (powers of 011 in octal spell Pascal's triangle until the carries), look-and-say, euclid-squares, spiral, karnaugh (Gray code turns AND terms into rectangles), cistercian-numerals, drum-machine (x*y % 8 < y gives Euclidean rhythms), ascii-vowels.

Middle (B/B+): houndstooth (a 2/2 twill weave), norway, lighthouse, hourglass, tanzania, paperfolding.

Weaker Monday fillers (B- to C+): swiss, rocket, mountains, coffee, launch-calendar, binary-carries.

Scheduling notes:

  • Traps: none. The only one is mild, in octal-pascal: reading 011 as decimal eleven is 28 cells off. It is the same octal mechanism as zero-padded and octal-modulo.
  • Octal literals: octal-pascal, calculator-hi and cistercian-numerals use them, as do the existing font-42 and several dailies. Spread these out.
  • Bitwise budget (two a week): octal-pascal, calculator-hi, karnaugh, binary-tree-maze, cistercian-numerals and ascii-vowels count.
  • Circles: greenland counts toward one every two weeks.
  • Tap-heavy (one a week): octal-pascal, binary-carries and drum-machine. Jamaica, tanzania and south-africa have about 12-16 diagonal taps each.
  • Norway has its cross where daily 5 (Danish flag) has one, so schedule it far from #5.

Tried and dropped because they don't read at 8x8 or are noise: Saturn with rings, tangram, DNA, Bayer dithering, hitomezashi, rule 90/150, LZ77 (no picture fits in 12 lines), frogger, perspective floor.

specials round 2

I designed a special for all 7 required dates plus one proposed extra date, Fibonacci Day (Nov 23).

The checker output is in final-check.txt; drafts and the naive-reading variants of the two traps are in drafts/.

The two traps

  • April Fools: c =+ 1 is c = +1, not c += 1. No daily or pool level uses this mechanism yet, and gcc gives no warning. The naive reading paints a purple fish with a blue eye, 34 cells off; the true grid is a white paper April fish.
  • Halloween: it uses the "OCT 31 == DEC 25" joke. Because 031 is octal for 25, the Christmas-tree branch never runs and the grid is a jack-o'-lantern. The naive reading paints a green tree, 55 cells off. Octal itself is not a new mechanism: dailies 35 and 46 and the pool's zero-padded level already use it.

Things the scheduler has to handle

  1. Year-1 puzzle numbers: Oct 31 is #27, Nov 23 is #50, Dec 25 is #82, Jan 1 is #89, Feb 14 is #133, Mar 14 is #161, Apr 1 is #179, and Sep 13 is #344. Pool levels 27 and 82 (and 50 if Fibonacci Day starts in 2026) are therefore skipped in the first loop.
  2. Ghost (daily 27): it is a Pac-Man ghost that fits any day, so it can stay in the pool.
  3. Tree (daily 82): a Christmas tree would come back on a random date in later loops, and my fir is within 4 cells of its silhouette. Retire it from the pool (or use it as the Christmas special instead of mine).
  4. Programmers' Day: the 256th day is Sep 12 in leap years. Consider pinning that special to day-of-year 256 rather than 09-13.
  5. Fibonacci Day: in 2026 it would skip daily 50, so it could start in 2027. Tau Day (06-28) is the alternative extra date if you would rather fill the April to September gap.
  6. Traps on neighboring days: where possible, keep pool traps off the days next to Halloween and April Fools.

Difficulty: the heart is 1, April Fools and Halloween are 3, the rest are 2. Every special is a picture you recognize once painted, and none is heavy to paint (at most about 25 actions).

Sources

There is plenty of material beyond bitwise operations. I built 26 new levels from outside sources, and all 26 pass the real level checker. Almost none use bitwise operators: only rule 30 and Life use a small lookup or neighbor count. An automatic comparison found no near-duplicates of the tutorial or the 12 dailies, allowing for mirrors, rotations and recoloring. The closest is corner-rainbow, 12 cells away from tutorial 5, which is the point of that trap.

The levels fall into eight families:

  • Geometry (Pythagoras, square root, Thales): corner-rainbow (a loop computes the square root, so no floats are needed), thales-venn (two overlapping circles from dot products), pac-man, queen-and-knight (a knight move is exactly dx*dx + dy*dy == 5).
  • Number theory: euclid-orchard (gcd by recursion), times-mod-7 (a black frame around a grid where every row and column is a permutation of 1 to 6), tartan, index-mod-7, primes, fibonacci-mod-8 (rows repeat every 3), hanoi-ruler.
  • Recursion and fractals: thue-morse, sierpinski-carpet, pascal-mod-3, rule-30.
  • Games and simulations: minesweeper, life (one generation), ghost, bubble-sort (one row per pass).
  • Art from instructions: lewitt-quarters, mondrian-unsigned.
  • Encodings: rle-heart, octal-sailboat.
  • C traps: mondrian-unsigned (unsigned wraparound), remainder-sign (% with a negative number), octal-sailboat (a leading 0 means octal), transpose-trap (a[x][y] flips the picture).
  • Seasonal: ghost fits #27 (Oct 31), christmas-tree #82 (Dec 25), rle-heart #133 (Feb 14).

How well the sources fit:

  • Best: tixy.land, OEIS-style number patterns, classic games, code-golf shapes, LeWitt and Mondrian, and C-trap books.
  • Weak: dwitter, PICO-8 tweetcarts and bytebeat are almost all animation, trig, random or audio. Only a few ideas carried over: pictures packed into numbers, Life, rule tables.
  • Dropped: 10 PRINT mazes read as checkerboard noise at 8x8. XOR textures and munching squares are already used up by dailies #2, #3 and #4, which is where the "too bitwise" feeling comes from.

Your idea of allowing char, string or float: I don't think it's needed.

  • octal-sailboat already packs a picture into numbers, one octal digit per cell color, which is what strings would have offered.
  • corner-rainbow covers "sqrt(9) = 3" with integers.
  • If you do add strings, allow only indexing and comparison to character literals (e.g. "..##"[x] == '#', or digits of pi with - '0'). Arithmetic on letters needs the ASCII table, which breaks mental computation.
  • None of the 26 levels needs a rule change.

Which C traps the compiler allows: I tested them against the level checker. Rejected: mixing & or | with == without parentheses, a < b < c, a dangling else, misleading indentation, assignment inside if. Accepted: unsigned wraparound, negative %, octal literals, 1 + y > 3 ? 2 : 4 precedence, a loop variable shadowing y, the --> "operator", and switch fallthrough when marked with a // fall through comment. So around eight trap mechanisms are available; spread them out.

What to watch:

  • rule-30 is the hardest (about 8 minutes) and doesn't draw a recognizable picture.
  • tartan, index-mod-7, remainder-sign and times-mod-7 are one-liners where every cell has to be tapped on a phone.
  • Two pairs share a skeleton: minesweeper and life, index-mod-7 and times-mod-7. Keep each pair far apart. Pac-man and ghost could run on consecutive days as a mini-story.
  • transpose-trap is the same family as #11 and #12, so keep it far from both.

The files are in /tmp/claude-1000/-home-lucien-dev-draw-my-code/6539cb5f-e2be-4d0a-a035-bf4a959a1c91/scratchpad/daily-design/research/:

  • 01-euclid-orchard.c to 26-transpose-trap.c
  • final-check.txt (the checker's output for all 26)
  • top-*.json and top.json (the 500 most-liked dweets)
  • tixy.html (the page source with its built-in examples)
  • probe/ (the trap tests)

Nothing in the repo was modified.

  1. Dwitter (top 500 dweets by awesome count)

    About 26,000 JavaScript canvas demos of 140 characters. The old /api/dweets endpoint ignores ordering; /apiv2beta/dweets/?order_by=-awesome_count works. Almost all are time-animated trig, particles or raymarching on a 1920x1080 canvas. The integer idioms worth taking: bitmaps packed into strings with charCodeAt(i/16)>>i%16&1 (p01 d/5600, RomanW d/5271, FireFly d/1502), Game of Life (pavel d/18291 'Keep Gliding Mr Conway'), rule-number automata (KilledByAPixel d/25270 'Defautomaton'), checkerboards with n%2^m%2 (sigveseb d/701), Sierpinski with &, and i&-n to round down (pavel d/18235 #breakout).

    Low for most content: it depends on time, sin/cos, floats and huge canvases, none of which survive 8x8 with integers and no time. Medium for the few integer idioms above. They inspired the RLE heart, the octal sailboat (packed pixels), Life and rule 30. Treat it as a source of flavor, not a level mine.

  2. tixy.land (Martin Kleppe)

    16x16 dots driven by one JS expression (t,i,x,y) of 32 characters or fewer. The ~40 built-in examples sit in the page's inline examples.json. Relevant ones: 'hungry pac man' (hypot(x-=t%4*5,y-=8)<6&&x<y|y<-x), 'mondrian squares' ((y-6)*(x-6)), grid (x%4&&y%4), frame, diagonals, 'sierpinski' (4*t&i&x&y), 'binary clock', 'scrolling TIXY font' ([5463,2194,2386][y+t*9&7]&1<<x-1, rows packed in decimal numbers), 'space invader' (column bytes from a string), '3d checker board' (perspective via (x-8)/y).

    High: the closest cousin. But half the examples need t or sin, and tixy draws size and sign, not 8 colors. Sierpinski and grid lines are already dailies #2 and #8. Pac-Man transfers perfectly (the Pac-Man and ghost candidates). The packed-font idea became the octal sailboat, and the index parameter i became index-mod-7. Perspective floors don't read on 8x8.

  3. HAKMEM item 146: munching squares, XOR textures

    PDP-1 display hack (1962, MIT AI Memo 239) that plots y = x XOR t for successive t. Variants: munching triangles (AND), and XOR textures such as (x^y)%9.

    High but already used up: a munching-squares snapshot is x^y (daily #3), munching triangles are x&y (daily #2), and daily #4 is an XOR bit checker. XOR textures need 256x256 to look good. No new levels recommended from here; it is the source of the 'too bitwise' feeling.

  4. 10 PRINT CHR$(205.5+RND(1)) and Truchet tiles

    The one-line Commodore 64 maze (and the MIT Press book about it): each character cell randomly gets a / or \ diagonal.

    Poor. On 8x8 each tile gets at most 2x2 cells, and 2-cell diagonals read as checkerboard noise, not a maze. I tested 6 variants with a hand-made LCG as RND. It also needs randomness, which becomes grinding. Dropped.

  5. Sol LeWitt wall drawings

    Conceptual art written as instructions for others to execute. The vocabulary is four kinds of lines (vertical, horizontal, diagonal right, diagonal left), for example 'Wall divided horizontally and vertically into four equal parts. Within each part, four kinds of lines are superimposed.'

    Good. An instruction that a program executes is exactly this game, and the four line kinds map to x%k, y%k, (x+y)%k and (x-y)%k. Used for lewitt-quarters. Superimposing all four line kinds as OR-ed color flags works but gives a dense 7-color chore.

  6. Piet Mondrian compositions

    Black grid lines with red, blue and yellow panels on white.

    High. The palette has white, black, red, blue and yellow, and the panels are made of long runs, so it is cheap to paint. Used for mondrian-unsigned, combined with the unsigned range-check trap.

  7. Vera Molnar: (Des)Ordres, Interruptions

    Plotter art (1968 to 1974): concentric squares or line grids disrupted by random displacement, rotation or erasure. The theme is order versus disorder.

    Medium-low. The order part (concentric squares) is already daily #5, and the disorder needs randomness. The transferable idea is design, not a picture: a regular pattern with one deliberate interruption that the player must find. That is the spirit of the unsigned and remainder traps.

  8. OEIS and classic number patterns

    Integer sequences with structure worth discovering: Thue-Morse (A010060), ruler function (A001511), Pisano periods (A001175, pi(8) = 12), primes (A000040), gcd tables and Euclid's orchard, Pascal's triangle mod p, squares mod 8, multiplication mod a prime.

    Very high and nearly endless. Map through n = 8y + x (a linear index, like tixy's i) or a 2D table f(x, y). The best ones have a shortcut (8 = 1 mod 7, odd squares = 1 mod 8, period 12 = 1.5 rows) that turns 64 computations into a pattern. Source of 8 candidates.

  9. Elementary cellular automata (Wolfram rules)

    A row of cells evolves by a 3-cell rule table. Rule 30 is chaotic, rule 90 is Sierpinski, rule 110 grows to one side.

    Good as the hardest tier. Recursion on y with f's own values is allowed and fast (3^7 calls). Rule 90 would duplicate daily #2, so I used rule 30. Mentally heavy (56 table lookups) and the result is not a recognizable picture.

  10. Conway's Game of Life

    Birth on 3 neighbors, survival on 2 or 3. Gliders, blinkers, still lifes.

    Good for one generation, encoded as before/after colors (dies, born, survives). Coordinate lists and a Chebyshev neighborhood keep it at 12 lines. More than one generation is too much to trace.

  11. Code golf and Rosetta Code shape tasks

    Classic ASCII-art tasks: Sierpinski carpet, Christmas tree, chessboard, diamond, Ulam spiral, spiral matrix.

    High for shape levels (carpet, tree). The Ulam spiral and spiral matrix don't fit 12 lines of 36 columns. The carpet needs 9x9, so an 8x8 crop loses its last row and column.

  12. PICO-8 tweetcarts

    Lua demos of 280 characters on a 128x128, 16-color machine: plasma (sin sums), fire (pget feedback), Monte Carlo random pixels, palette remapping.

    Low. Almost everything is time, sin, random or read-back of the screen. Salvageable: feedback maps to recursion on f(x, y-1) (as in rule 30 and Pascal), palette remapping to a color lookup array, and x*x+y*y moire to the tartan level.

  13. Bytebeat (viznut, 2011)

    One-line C expressions of a time counter t that output 8-bit audio, for example t*(t>>5|t>>8).

    Poor. The output is 1D, the patterns need t in the thousands, the formulas are bitwise-heavy, and they can't be computed in your head. Only the idea of a single linear index i = 8y+x survives, used in index-mod-7, primes, RLE, Hanoi and Fibonacci.

  14. C puzzle and trap literature (Feuer, The C Puzzle Book; Koenig, C Traps and Pitfalls)

    Expression-evaluation puzzles about precedence, conversions, operators and declarations.

    High for trap levels, but the build flags filter it hard. I probed with check-level.ts. Rejected by -Wall -Wextra -Werror: & or | mixed with == (-Wparentheses), a<b<c, dangling else, misleading indentation, assignment in if, unused comma operands. Survivors, all tested: unsigned wraparound, % with negative operands, octal literals, ?: versus + precedence (1 + y > 3 ? 2 : 4), a[x][y] order, a loop variable shadowing y, the '-->' operator, and switch fallthrough when marked with a '// fall through' comment.

  15. Classic games: chess, Minesweeper, Pac-Man

    Universally known 8x8-friendly boards and sprites.

    High. Chess is natively 8x8, and a knight move is exactly dx*dx + dy*dy == 5. Minesweeper numbers are small colors, and Pac-Man and the ghost are iconic at 8x8. Gives both an aha ('it's Minesweeper!') and a good-looking share grid.

  16. Geometry: Pythagoras and Thales

    Integer distances (3-4-5), the integer square root, and the sign of the dot product PA.PB, which is negative inside, zero on, and positive outside the circle with diameter AB.

    High, as the owner suspected. Dot products split into a column term plus a row term, so a 2-circle Venn costs 16 small numbers to compute. A single Thales circle on 8x8 is exactly daily #1's disk plus a 12-point rim, so avoid it. The integer square root by loop covers 'sqrt(9) = 3' without floats.
